Abstract: Lithium metal batteries possess the high theoretical specific energy owing to the high

theoretical specific capacity of lithium metal. However, practical implementations necessitate a

reduction in both lithium mass fraction and lithium utilization within the negative electrode to

enhance cycling life and suppress dendrite formation, resulting in a practical reversible capacity

of only 30 – 50% of the theoretical value. Herein, we present a lithium metal-based

multicomponent solid-solution alloy comprising approximately 90 wt.% lithium, with equal

atomic ratios of cadmium, silver, magnesium, and aluminium constituting the remaining 10 wt.%.

The increased mixing entropy enables high lithium-atom diffusivity, facilitating inward lithium

transport into the metal foil rather than the surface deposition typically observed in conventional

lithium metal negative electrodes, while simultaneously promoting a thermodynamically stable

(110) crystal facet. These factors collectively yield a dendrite-free negative electrode with a

reversible specific capacity of 3100 mAh g−1. One-ampere-hour pouch cells employing this

negative electrode and a LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 positive electrode achieve an specific energies of 385

Wh kg−1 (based on the total mass of the pouch cell) with 82% capacity retention over 600 cycles.

This achievement highlights the potential of this alloy negative electrode to enable safe and durable

high-energy-density lithium metal batteries for practical applications.

## 1. Introduction

The pursuit of high-energy-density batteries for emerging electric aircraft and other

advancements in the low-altitude economy has stimulated a significant increase in research on Li

metal batteries (LMBs) owing to the high theoretical specific capacity (3860 mAh g−1) and the

lowest redox potential (−3.04 V versus the standard hydrogen electrode) of Li metal negative

electrode.1,2 Current investigations have predominantly centered on the challenges posed by

uncontrolled Li dendrite growth, which results in low Coulombic efficiency (CE), poor cycle life

expectancy, and potential safety hazards due to internal short-circuiting.3,4 In an effort to mitigate

Li dendrite formation and extend the batteries' cycle life, a variety of extensive strategies have

been employed, including the optimization of electrolytes and additives,5,6 the development of

artificial protective layers,7,8 the utilization of three-dimensional host scaffolds,9 and the

incorporation of Li-Ag binary solid-solution alloy.10,11

In the practical application of LMBs, it is imperative to not only address the challenges

associated with Li dendrites and battery life span but also consider the Li mass fraction within the

electrode (M) and Li utilization (U) during cycling. These factors directly determine the achievable

practical specific capacity of the Li metal negative electrode, which can be expressed

mathematically as: Practical specific capacity =  3860 mAh/g ×  M × U.12 Current designs of

Li metal electrodes compromise Li mass fraction, which is below 60 wt.%, or Li utilization, which

is below 80 %, in an effort to extend cycling life and avoid the Li dendrite (Fig. 1a and

Supplementary Table 1).11,13-22 This trade-off results in a practical capacity typically below 2000

mAh g−1, thereby diminishing the inherent advantage of Li metal's high specific capacity.

Consequently, LMBs still suffered from the unsatisfactory trade-off between specific energy and

cycling life (Fig. 1b).14,15,22-33 Taking a 10 Ah Li||LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 pouch cell as an example,

the positive electrode employs a standard commercial positive electrode with an areal capacity of

compatibility among the elements, thereby preventing phase separation and mitigating the

formation of intermetallic compounds, which facilitates the establishment of a solid-solution-

based metal alloy phase. The Li-MSSA presents rapid Li atom diffusion throughout the bulk of the

thickness of the Li-MSSA foil. The ampere-hour level Li-metal pouch cells, comprising the

configuration Li-MSSA||LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2, achieve a balance of high specific energy and

excellent cycling performance.

in comparison to intermetallic compounds. This characteristic results in markedly enhanced

reversibility and cycling stability during the Li-alloying/dealloying process, as the solid-solution

reaction accommodates a degree of stoichiometric tolerance to variations in Li atom concentrations

Ag, Mg, and Cd, which are recognized for their broad solid solution ranges with Li atoms, as

alloying constituents.35-37 Given the diverse melting points and compatibilities of Mg, Ag, and Cd,

Al was chosen as a "binder" due to its negative enthalpy of mixing,38 which promotes a high

chemical affinity among distinct atomic species and guarantees the homogeneous dispersion of

metallic components. The Li-MSSA was synthesized by heating a mixture of Li, Cd, Ag, Mg, and

Al metallic powders at 600 °C under mechanical stirring in an argon-filled glovebox (see Methods

section for detail). The resultant Li-MSSA comprises 90 wt.% metallic Li, with Cd, Ag, Mg, and

Al making up the remaining 10 wt.% in an equal atomic ratio of 1:1:1:1 (Supplementary Fig. 2

findings illustrate the electrochemical performance of our Li-MSSA electrode, ensures a high Li

therefore employed a non-ideal, chemical-potential-based diffusion formulation to fit the full

10−9 cm2 s−1 (Supplementary Fig. 16). As expected, applying other analysis routes to the same

dataset — such as the traditional GITT early-time √τ approximation, or EIS-based diffusivity

extraction — yields values up to one or two orders of magnitude higher relative to our non-ideal,

chemical-potential-driven fit.40 Notably, these values are higher than the reported room-

temperature self-diffusion of Li in metallic Li (typically 10−11 cm2 s−1).41 Taken together, the fitted

D is sufficiently high to accommodate the per-pulse Li flux by bulk insertion into Li-MSSA. We

believe that the elevated diffusion coefficient of Li atoms in Li-MSSA is attributable to the diverse

pathways available for Li atom diffusion, which arise from the increased configurational entropy

of the Li-MSSA. With a greater variety of configurations, multiple diffusion pathways, presumably

characterized by lower energy barriers, are available, thereby enhancing the kinetics of Li atom

diffusion.42 Therefore, it is the high Li atom diffusion coefficient inherent in Li-MSSA that

facilitates Li atom transfer into the foil, as opposed to surface plating of Li during lithiation process,

despite the the framework mass constituting only ~10 wt.% of the entire electrode.

Unlike the widely used “lithiophilic site” strategy — where alloy additives mainly lower the

Li nucleation overpotential to promote more uniform Li deposition45-47 — our alloy is designed to

promote an inward-growth mode, in which Li atoms migrate into the bulk rather than accumulate

at the interface10,11. In the lithiophilic approach, once a thin Li layer forms, subsequent cycling still

proceeds by Li+ reduction on Li metal at the electrolyte interface; the locus of deposition does not

fundamentally change. By contrast, our multicomponent solid solution operates as a single phase

with finite Li solubility, so the Li chemical potential varies continuously with composition. Under

plating, this establishes a chemical-potential gradient that drives freshly formed Li atoms at the

surface to diffuse inward rather than accumulate at the interface — consistent with solid-solution-

assisted inward growth.10,11 Kinetically, multicomponent solid-solution alloys (≥5 elements)

possess high configurational entropy that induces significant local chemical and strain disorder,

deposition. Consistent with this mechanism, our in-situ XRD, TOF-SIMS, and STEM-EDX/EELS

## 3. Discussion

In summary, we have developed a negative electrode comprising metallic Li-based

multicomponent solid-solution alloy, Li-MSSA, aimed to achieve the practical high-energy-

density and durable LMBs. The elevated mixing entropy induced by the multi-metal components

of Li-MSSA facilitates rapid Li atom diffusion throughout the bulk of the metal foil, rendering

inward transfer of Li atoms into the metal foil, as opposed to mere surface deposition, while also

promoting the thermodynamically stable (110) crystal facet. Collectively, these effects enable Li-

MSSA to maintain a dendrite-free, long-term cycling performance, characterized by both a high

Li mass ratio and high Li utilization, ultimately yielding a high reversible specific capacity of 3100

mAh g−1. Consequently, the Ah-level pouch cell achieves a specific energy of 385 Wh kg−1 (based

on the total mass of the pouch cell) and retains 82% of its capacity over 600 cycles.

The heating-rolling methodology employed for preparing Li-MSSA is consistent with

industrial-scale metal processing standards. This process yields Li-MSSA foils with lengths of

several tens of meters and thicknesses ranging from tens to hundreds of micrometers, enabling

tunable calculated areal capacities, which provides a considerable range for optimizing battery

design — a critical considerable in industrial engineering. The Li-MSSA negative electrode is

compatible with positive electrodes of varying chemistries, including Li-rich manganese and

sulfur-based positive electrodes, as well as with electrolytes in both liquid and solid states. This

versatility highlights the scalability of Li-MSSA for practical LMBs, positioning it as a promising

candidate for practical applications, such as emerging electric aircraft in the low-altitude economy.

Future research can focus on selecting the contents by incorporating diverse elements or expanding

the range of elements within the Li-MSSA to further enhance its electrochemical and mechanical

performance. In parallel, it will be important to elucidate the physical origin of the bcc solid-

solution stability down to low Li content, through quantitative mapping of the composition-

## 4. Methods

Material Synthesis

The Li-MSSA composite was synthesized by heating a mixture of Li, Cd, Ag, Mg, and Al metallic

powders to 600 °C at a ramp rate of 5 °C min−1, followed by holding at 600 °C for 2 h under

mechanical stirring in an argon-filled glovebox, where the O2 and H2O levels were maintained

below 0.01 ppm. The final composite comprises 90 wt.% lithium, with Cd, Ag, Mg, and Al

constituting the remaining 10 wt.% in an equimolar ratio (1:1:1:1). Subsequently, the molten

mixture was rapidly cooled to −196 °C by immersion in liquid nitrogen, resulting in a dense, grey

solid. This solid was then sectioned and rolled to the desired thickness in a dry room with a dew

point below −40 °C. Notably, for film thicknesses below 10 μm, rolling was not feasible; instead,

a melting and casting approach was employed to achieve the specified dimensions. Lithium foil

(Li, 99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich), cadmium granules (Cd, ≥99%, Aladdin; purchased via the

CASMART procurement platform), silver powder (Ag, ≥99.99% trace metals basis, Sigma-

Aldrich), magnesium powder (Mg, ≥99.9% trace metals basis, Sigma-Aldrich), and aluminum foil

(Al, ≥99.99% trace metals basis, Sigma-Aldrich) were used as received unless otherwise noted.

Editorial Summary Lithium-metal batteries promise high energy but dendrites limit life. Here, authors introduce a 90 wt.% lithium multicomponent solid solution alloy negative electrode that drives lithium into the bulk, enabling 3100 mAh g−1 capacity and a 385 Wh kg−1 pouch cell that retains 82% capacity after 600 cycles.
